faq.a: Sodium determines plasma osmolality, drives water movement, and maintains ECF volume.
faq.q: Why is sodium the principal extracellular cation?

faq.a: Yes for mild‑moderate dehydration; IV is required for severe hypovolaemia, shock, or when oral intake is impossible.
faq.q: Can oral rehydration replace IV fluids?

faq.a: Rapid rise can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome, leading to irreversible neurologic injury.
faq.q: What is the danger of correcting chronic hyponatraemia too fast?

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with severe cholera presents with 12 L diarrhoea in 24 h – what is your immediate fluid plan and why? — Give isotonic saline bolus 20 mL/kg, reassess vitals, then switch to ORS once stable; sodium replacement is essential to restore ECF volume.

A patient on anti‑TB therapy develops peripheral oedema and hypertension – which electrolyte abnormality should you suspect and how would you confirm it? — Suspect hypernatraemia from excessive saline; check serum Na+; treat by adjusting fluid type.

How does point‑of‑care ultrasound differentiate hypovolaemia from hypervolaemia? — IVC collapsibility >50 % indicates low intravascular volume; a plethoric IVC with hepatic vein congestion suggests fluid overload.

Why is balanced crystalloid preferred over normal saline in large‑volume resuscitation for severe malaria? — Balanced solutions contain less chloride, reducing risk of hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis common in massive saline infusions.

A child with sickle cell disease presents with vaso‑occlusive crisis and low urine output – what fluid strategy avoids worsening sickling? — Use isotonic saline cautiously; avoid rapid over‑hydration that may cause pulmonary oedema, monitor electrolytes closely.

What red‑flag sign would prompt you to call senior staff in a patient with suspected hypernatraemia? — New onset seizures or decreased consciousness indicates severe hypernatraemia requiring urgent specialist input.
ai.title: Extracellular Fluid Balance
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Extracellular fluid (ECF) volume and composition are tightly regulated by sodium, water, and hormones. Disruption leads to oedema, dehydration, or electrolyte disorders, which are common in low‑resource settings.

b: Measure blood pressure, pulse, skin turgor, and urine output.
Check serum Na+, K+, Cl‑, HCO3‑, Ca2+, PO4‑ and osmolality.
sections.p: ECF includes plasma and interstitial fluid that bathes cells. Clinically we assess volume (hypovolaemia, euvolaemia, hypervolaemia) and composition (sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate).

b: Mild: orthostatic drop ≤10 mmHg, urine <0.5 mL/kg/h.
Moderate: orthostatic drop 10‑20 mmHg, urine 0.3‑0.5 mL/kg/h.
Severe: orthostatic drop >20 mmHg, urine <0.3 mL/kg/h, altered mental status.
sections.p: Volume disturbances are staged by clinical signs and simple labs:

b: Gastro‑intestinal loss (cholera, dysentery, malaria‑related diarrhoea).
Renal loss (diuretic over‑use, acute tubular necrosis from severe malaria).
Third‑space loss (peritoneal TB, severe pneumonia, burns).
Excess intake (hypertonic saline infusions, herbal decoctions).
sections.p: In East African hospitals the common precipitants are:

b: Rapidly falling BP suggests severe dehydration or haemorrhage.
Pitting oedema in dependent limbs points to fluid overload.
sections.p: Hypovolaemia presents with tachycardia, low BP, dry mucosa, decreased skin turgor, and oliguria. Hypervolaemia shows peripheral oedema, raised JVP, crackles, and possibly hypertension.

t.b: Is the patient hyponatraemic, normonatraemic or hypernatraemic? Guides fluid type (isotonic vs hypotonic).
Detects K+ loss (diarrhoea, diuretics) or excess (renal failure). Influences choice of rehydration solution.
Assesses renal contribution to volume status; rising creatinine signals acute kidney injury.
Quantifies renal perfusion; <0.5 mL/kg/h suggests hypovolaemia or renal failure.
Looks for IVC collapsibility (hypovolaemia) or pleural effusions (hypervolaemia).

t.a: If ultrasound unavailable – bedside assessment of neck veins and lung sounds
t.b: Provides surrogate for volume status; flat neck veins and clear lungs favour hypovolaemia.

b: Severe hypovolaemia → shock, acute kidney injury, myocardial ischaemia.
Severe hypernatraemia → cerebral dehydration, seizures, coma.
Rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia → osmotic demyelination.
sections.p: Uncorrected ECF disturbances can rapidly become fatal.

b: Isotonic crystalloid (0.9 % saline) for hypovolaemia due to loss of Na+ and water.
Balanced solutions (Ringer's lactate) when large volumes needed and metabolic acidosis present.
Hypertonic saline (3 % NaCl) only for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia; avoid rapid >10 mmol/L rise in 24 h.
Potassium replacement (IV KCl) when serum K+ <3.5 mmol/L and urine output adequate.
Diuretics (loop) for hypervolaemia with pulmonary oedema; avoid if renal failure or severe hypovolaemia.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then restore volume and electrolyte balance.

b: Provide oral rehydration salts (ORS) for mild‑moderate dehydration.
Vaccinate against cholera and rotavirus where available.
Monitor chronic diseases (heart failure, CKD) that predispose to fluid overload.
sections.p: Re‑assess vitals, urine output, and electrolytes every 4‑6 h until stable. Educate patients on safe fluid intake, early treatment of diarrhoea, and avoiding excessive herbal fluids.

b: Anemia – can cause tachycardia but does not change fluid volume.
Septic shock – may present with warm extremities and low BP but is driven by vasodilation, not pure volume loss.
Serum sodium may appear normal in hyperglycaemia; correct using Na_corrected = Na_measured + 1.6 × [(glucose‑100)/100].
Urine output can be low in early hypovolaemia despite adequate intravascular volume if renal perfusion is delayed.
sections.p: Lab values may be deceptive in certain settings.

whenToSeekHelp: Unresponsive patient with suspected severe electrolyte disturbance.
Rapidly rising serum sodium (>150 mmol/L) or falling (<120 mmol/L).
